questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$, the transformation matrix $P$ satisfies $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. What does multiplying $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ by $P$ do to the vector $\boldsymbol{x}$ itself?
options: Nothing: $\boldsymbol{x}$ stays the same vector and only its list of coordinates changes
It moves $\boldsymbol{x}$ to a new vector, the image of $\boldsymbol{x}$ under a linear map
It projects $\boldsymbol{x}$ onto the span of the new basis vectors $\boldsymbol{c}_1,\boldsymbol{c}_2$
It rotates $\boldsymbol{x}$ through the angle between $\boldsymbol{b}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{c}_1$

questions.question: In the space $P_1$ of real polynomials of degree at most $1$, take the ordered bases $\mathcal{B}=(1,t)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(1,1+t)$. Which matrix is $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}$, converting $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates?

For ordered bases $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the transformation matrix $P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=P_{\mathcal{C}\leftarrow\mathcal{B}}[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. A vector has $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=(1,1)^{\top}$. What is $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$?

In a three-dimensional space $V$ with ordered basis $\mathcal{C}$, a student takes vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_3=\boldsymbol{v}_1+\boldsymbol{v}_2$ and forms $M=\big([\boldsymbol{v}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}\ [\boldsymbol{v}_2]_{\mathcal{C}}\ [\boldsymbol{v}_3]_{\mathcal{C}}\big)$ to use as a transformation matrix. Which statement about $M$ is correct?
options: $M$ is invertible, because its columns are coordinates in the basis $\mathcal{C}$
$M$ is singular, yet every vector has unique coordinates with respect to the list
$M$ is singular, and coordinates with respect to the list are not unique
$M$ has a zero third column, because the vector $\boldsymbol{v}_3$ is redundant

questions.question: Let $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{b}_1,\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3)$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{b}_2,\boldsymbol{b}_3,\boldsymbol{b}_1)$ the same vectors in a cyclically shifted order. If $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(1,2,3)^{\top}$, what is $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$?

Two ordered bases of $\mathbb{R}^2$ are $\mathcal{B}=\big((1,1)^{\top},(1,-1)^{\top}\big)$ and $\mathcal{C}=\big((1,0)^{\top},(1,1)^{\top}\big)$, with vectors in standard coordinates. Find $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ for the vector whose $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates are $[\boldsymbol{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(1,2)^{\top}$.
